claim: COVID-19 pathogenesis is associated with a hyperinflammatory response.
source: The pathogenesis of COVID-19 is associated with a hyperinflammatory response; however, the precise mechanism of SARS-CoV-2-induced inflammation is poorly understood.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established fact about COVID-19 pathogenesis.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 spike protein induces inflammatory cytokines and chemokines including IL-6, IL-1β, TNFα, CXCL1, CXCL2, and CCL2 in human and mouse macrophages.
source: We observed that spike (S) protein potently induced inflammatory cytokines and chemokines, including IL-6, IL-1β, TNFα, CXCL1, CXCL2, and CCL2, but not IFNs in human and mouse macrophages.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including RT-PCR and ELISA measurements shown in Figure 1.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 spike protein does not induce interferons in human and mouse macrophages.
source: We observed that spike (S) protein potently induced inflammatory cytokines and chemokines, including IL-6, IL-1β, TNFα, CXCL1, CXCL2, and CCL2, but not IFNs in human and mouse macrophages.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing no induction of IFNA, IFNB, or IFNG in response to S protein stimulation (Figure 1A).

claim: Membrane (M), envelope (E), and nucleocapsid (N) proteins of SARS-CoV-2 do not induce inflammatory responses in macrophages.
source: No such inflammatory response was observed in response to membrane (M), envelope (E), and nucleocapsid (N) proteins.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A where M, N, and E proteins failed to induce cytokines and chemokines.

claim: Human and mouse lung epithelial cells produce inflammatory cytokines and chemokines when stimulated with extracellular S protein.
source: When stimulated with extracellular S protein, human and mouse lung epithelial cells also produced inflammatory cytokines and chemokines.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 2 showing cytokine induction in A549, Calu3, and primary mouse lung epithelial cells.

claim: Epithelial cells expressing S protein intracellularly are non-inflammatory.
source: Interestingly, epithelial cells expressing S protein intracellularly were non-inflammatory, but elicited an inflammatory response in macrophages when co-cultured.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B-D showing no cytokine induction in S-transfected epithelial cells.

claim: Epithelial cells expressing S protein intracellularly elicit an inflammatory response in macrophages when co-cultured.
source: Interestingly, epithelial cells expressing S protein intracellularly were non-inflammatory, but elicited an inflammatory response in macrophages when co-cultured.
evidence: This is supported by co-culture experiments shown in Figure 3E-H demonstrating cytokine induction when S-expressing epithelial cells are co-cultured with THP1 cells.

claim: S protein triggers inflammation via activation of the NF-κB pathway in a MyD88-dependent manner.
source: Biochemical studies revealed that S protein triggers inflammation via activation of the NF-κB pathway in a MyD88-dependent manner.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data in Figure 4 showing NF-κB activation and Figure 5A-B showing loss of response in Myd88−/− macrophages.

claim: Activation of the NF-κB pathway by S protein is abrogated in Tlr2-deficient macrophages.
source: Further, such an activation of the NF-κB pathway was abrogated in Tlr2-deficient macrophages.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data in Figure 5C-D showing no NF-κB activation in Tlr2−/− macrophages stimulated with S protein.

claim: Administration of S protein induces IL-6, TNF-α, and IL-1β in wild-type mice but not Tlr2-deficient mice.
source: Consistently, administration of S protein-induced IL-6, TNF-α, and IL-1β in wild-type, but not Tlr2-deficient mice.
evidence: This is supported by in vivo data in Figure 5H showing elevated cytokines in WT but not Tlr2−/− mice after S protein administration.

claim: TLR2 dimerizes with TLR1 or TLR6 to activate the NF-κB pathway upon recognition of S protein.
source: Notably, upon recognition of S protein, TLR2 dimerizes with TLR1 or TLR6 to activate the NF-κB pathway.
evidence: This is supported by experiments with HEK-Blue cells expressing different TLR combinations (Figure 6) and CRISPR knockout studies (Figure 6G).

claim: SARS-CoV-2 is a positive sense single-stranded RNA virus.
source: SARS-CoV-2 is a positive sense single-stranded RNA virus.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the viral genome structure.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 primarily causes infection in the respiratory tract.
source: Like other coronaviruses, such as SARS (retrospectively named SARS-CoV-1) and Middle Eastern respiratory syndrome (MERS)-CoV, SARS-CoV-2 primarily causes infection in the respiratory tract, leading to either asymptomatic infection or a range of symptoms including cough, fever, pneumonia, respiratory failure, along with other complications like diarrhea and multi-organ failure (Vabret et al., 2020; Tay et al., 2020; Li et al., 2020; Gu et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: COVID-19 has caused over 4 million deaths worldwide by the end of 2021.
source: In the absence of effective therapies, COVID-19 has caused over 4 million deaths worldwide by the end of 2021.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the pandemic's impact based on epidemiological data.

claim: Immunopathology caused by the cytokine storm plays a decisive role in COVID-19 pathogenesis.
source: Although our knowledge is still evolving, immunopathology caused by the cytokine storm plays a decisive role in COVID-19 pathogenesis (Vabret et al., 2020; Tay et al., 2020; Blanco-Melo et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 infects human cells through its Spike protein binding to ACE2 receptor.
source: SARS-CoV-2 infects human cells through its Spike (S) protein, which binds to the receptor angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 (ACE2), expressed on alveolar epithelial cells, allowing endocytosis of the viral particle (Zhou et al., 2020b; Hoffmann et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Disease severity and death of COVID-19 patients have been correlated to elevated expression of IL-6 and TNFα.
source: Disease severity and death of COVID-19 patients have been correlated to the elevated expression of IL-6 and TNFα (Huang et al., 2020; Hadjadj et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: S2 subunit of spike protein is more potent than S1 in inducing proinflammatory cytokines in THP1 cells.
source: Interestingly, both S1 and S2 proteins induced proinflammatory cytokines IL6, TNFA, and IL1B, with S2 being more potent, as measured by real-time RT-PCR and ELISA (Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing S1 and S2 responses in Figure 1A.

claim: THP1 cells are not defective in producing interferons when activated by PolyI:C.
source: Notably, THP1 cells are not defective in producing interferons when activated by PolyI:C, a ligand for TLR3 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C showing interferon induction by PolyI:C.

claim: S1 and S2 exert a synergistic effect on cytokine production when cells are incubated with them together.
source: S1 and S2 exerted a synergistic effect on cytokine production when cells were incubated with them together (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: M, N, and E proteins have no effect on S-induced inflammatory responses.
source: However, other structural proteins, including M, N, and E, had no effect on S-induced inflammatory responses (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The expression of cytokines and chemokines in response to S protein is dose dependent.
source: The expression of cytokines and chemokines in response to S protein was dose dependent (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 1B showing dose-response curves.

claim: S protein-induced inflammatory response is time dependent, with highest response at 8 hr post stimulation.
source: Similarly, S protein-induced inflammatory response was time dependent, with highest being at 8 hr post stimulation (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 1C showing time-course measurements.

claim: Heat-denatured S2 protein fails to stimulate THP-1 cells.
source: Notably, heat-denatured S2 protein failed to stimulate THP-1 cells, confirming the specificity of S protein and the requirement of its native structural configuration in inducing inflammatory response (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D comparing native and heat-denatured S2.

claim: Trimeric S protein is immunostimulatory, producing cytokines and chemokines in THP1 cells.
source: Notably, trimeric S protein (S-tri) is also immunostimulatory, producing cytokines IL6 and IL1B, and chemokines CXCL1 and CXCL2 in THP1 cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Human peripheral blood mononuclear cells show robust induction of IL1B, IL6, TNFA, CXCL1, and CXCL2 in response to S2 protein.
source: There was robust induction of IL1B, IL6, TNFA, CXCL1, and CXCL2 in hPBMC at 4 hr post-stimulation (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 1D using human PBMCs.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 does not infect mouse cells since S protein does not bind with mouse ACE2 receptor.
source: SARS-CoV-2 does not infect mouse cells since S protein does not bind with mouse ACE2 receptor.
evidence: This is established knowledge about species-specific ACE2 binding.

claim: Mouse bone marrow-derived macrophages produce Il6, Il1b, Tnfa, Cxcl1 and Cxcl2 in response to S1 and S2 proteins.
source: Surprisingly, both S1 and S2 proteins triggered expression of Il6, Il1b, Tnfa, Cxcl1 and Cxcl2 in mBMDMs (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Mouse BMDMs do not produce type-I and type-II interferons in response to S protein.
source: Similar to THP1 cells, mBMDMs did not produce type-I and type-II interferons in response to S protein (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Inhibition of ACE2 does not affect cytokine production in response to S protein.
source: Interestingly, inhibition of ACE2 did not affect cytokine production in response to S protein (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 1E using ACE2 inhibitor MLN-4760.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 S protein induces proinflammatory cytokines and chemokines in macrophages and monocytes in an ACE2-independent manner.
source: Taken together, SARS-CoV-2 S protein induces proinflammatory cytokines and chemokines in macrophages and monocytes in an ACE2-independent manner.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experiments including mouse macrophage responses and ACE2 inhibition studies.

claim: S1 and S2 proteins induce proinflammatory cytokines and chemokines in A549 cells at 12 and 24 hr post-stimulation.
source: Interestingly, both S1 and S2 proteins induced proinflammatory cytokines IL6, IL1B, TNFA, and chemokines CXCL1 and CXCL2 with highest being at 24 hr post-stimulation (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 2A showing time-dependent responses in A549 cells.

claim: Calu3 cells produce IL6, IL1B, TNFA, CXCL1, and CXCL2 in response to S protein.
source: Similarly, Calu3 cells, a commonly used human lung epithelial cell line, and mouse primary lung epithelial cells produced IL6, IL1B, TNFA, CXCL1, and CXCL2 in response to S protein (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 2B.

claim: Mouse primary lung epithelial cells produce IL6, IL1B, TNFA, CXCL1, and CXCL2 in response to S protein.
source: Similarly, Calu3 cells, a commonly used human lung epithelial cell line, and mouse primary lung epithelial cells produced IL6, IL1B, TNFA, CXCL1, and CXCL2 in response to S protein (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 2C.

claim: IL-1β, IL-6, and TNFα protein levels are elevated in Calu3 and primary lung epithelial cells in response to S protein.
source: We confirmed the expression of IL-1β, IL-6, and TNFα at protein levels in Calu3 and primary lung epithelial cells by ELISA (Figure 2D and E).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data in Figure 2D and E.

claim: Cytosolic S protein does not induce cytokines and chemokines in A549, Calu3, and HEK293T cells.
source: However, cytosolic S protein did not induce any cytokines and chemokines in A549, Calu3, and HEK293T cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B-D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B-D showing no cytokine induction in S-transfected cells.

claim: Culture supernatants of epithelial cells expressing S protein fail to induce cytokines in THP1 cells.
source: However, culture supernatants of epithelial cells expressing S protein failed to induce cytokines IL6, IL1B, and TNFA in THP1 cells (Figure 3B and C, and Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 3B, C and Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claim: S protein is not detectable in the culture supernatant of HEK293T and A549 cells expressing S protein.
source: In fact, S protein was not detectable in the culture supernatant of HEK293T and A549 cells expressing S protein (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B.

claim: S protein is primarily located in the cytoplasm, not on the cell surface of transfected cells.
source: Flow cytometric analysis suggested that S protein is primarily located in the cytoplasm, not on the cell surface (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 3—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Inflammatory cytokines are induced when S protein-expressing epithelial cells are co-cultured with THP1 cells.
source: Interestingly, inflammatory cytokines were induced in co-cultured cells (Figure 3E and F, and Figure 3—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 3E, F and Figure 3—figure supplement 2D.

claim: Lysates of HEK293T-S cells efficiently induce inflammatory cytokines in THP1 cells.
source: Lysates of HEK293T-S cells efficiently induced inflammatory cytokines in THP1 cells while no such induction was observed in response to cell lysate of HEK293T-GFP cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 2G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 3—figure supplement 2G.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 infected epithelial cells may stimulate macrophages and monocytes in a paracrine manner to produce inflammatory mediators.
source: Taken together, these data imply that SARS-CoV-2 infected epithelial cells may stimulate macrophages and monocytes in a paracrine manner to produce inflammatory mediators.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from co-culture and cell lysate experiments.

claim: P65 and IκB are phosphorylated in THP1 cells treated with S2 protein.
source: As shown in Figure 4A, P65 and IκB were phosphorylated in cells treated with S2.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data in Figure 4A.

claim: There is no activation of ERK and JNK in S2 stimulated THP1 cells.
source: Surprisingly, there was no activation of ERK and JNK in S2 stimulated cells (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data in Figure 4A showing no phosphorylation of ERK and JNK.

claim: There is no activation of the AKT pathway in S2 stimulated THP1 cells.
source: There was also no activation of the AKT pathway (Figure 4A), but STAT3 was phosphorylated at 2 hr following stimulation (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data in Figure 4A showing no AKT phosphorylation.

claim: STAT3 is phosphorylated at 2 hr following S2 stimulation in THP1 cells.
source: There was also no activation of the AKT pathway (Figure 4A), but STAT3 was phosphorylated at 2 hr following stimulation (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data in Figure 4A showing STAT3 phosphorylation.

claim: S2 protein activates the NF-κB and STAT3 pathways in A549 cells.
source: S2 protein also activated the NF-κB and STAT3 pathways in A549 cells (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data in Figure 4B.

claim: Inhibition of the NF-κB pathway abrogates inflammatory responses in S protein-stimulated macrophages.
source: As expected, inhibition of the NF-κB pathway abrogated inflammatory responses in S protein-stimulated macrophages (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 4C and D using IKKβ inhibitor sc514.

claim: There is no activation of the NF-κB pathway in Myd88−/− BMDM stimulated with S2.
source: Interestingly, there was no activation of the NF-κB pathway in Myd88−/− BMDM (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data in Figure 5A showing no P65 and IκBα phosphorylation in Myd88−/− cells.

claim: There is no cytokine expression in Myd88−/− macrophages upon stimulation with S2 protein.
source: Consistently, there was no cytokine expression in Myd88−/− macrophages upon stimulation with S2 protein (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data in Figure 5B.

claim: S protein-mediated activation of NF-κB involves TLR/MyD88 signaling axis.
source: This observation suggests that S protein-mediated activation of the transcription factor NF-κB involves TLR/MyD88 signaling axis.
evidence: This is inferred from the loss of NF-κB activation and cytokine production in Myd88−/− macrophages.

claim: There is no activation of the NF-κB pathway in Tlr2−/− BMDM stimulated with S2.
source: There was no activation of the NF-κB pathway in Tlr2−/− BMDM, while activation of this pathway was intact in Tlr4−/− macrophages (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data in Figure 5C showing no NF-κB activation in Tlr2−/− but normal activation in Tlr4−/− cells.

claim: Activation of the NF-κB pathway is intact in Tlr4−/− macrophages stimulated with S2.
source: There was no activation of the NF-κB pathway in Tlr2−/− BMDM, while activation of this pathway was intact in Tlr4−/− macrophages (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data in Figure 5C showing normal NF-κB activation in Tlr4−/− cells.

claim: S1 protein activates the NF-κB pathway in WT macrophages but not Tlr2−/− macrophages.
source: Similar to S2, S1 protein activated the NF-κB pathway in WT macrophages but not Tlr2−/− macrophages (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data in Figure 5D.

claim: There is no induction of proinflammatory cytokines in S-stimulated Tlr2−/− macrophages.
source: Consistent to the defective activation of the NF-κB pathway, there was no induction of proinflammatory cytokines in S-stimulated Tlr2−/− macrophages (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data in Figure 5E.

claim: S-tri is sensed by TLR2, but not TLR4.
source: Notably, similar to S protein, S-tri is also sensed by TLR2, but not TLR4, as Tlr2−/− macrophages failed to induce cytokines in response to S-tri, while no such defect in inflammatory response was observed in Tlr4−/− macrophages (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 5F comparing responses in Tlr2−/− and Tlr4−/− macrophages.

claim: Inhibition of TLR2 by C29 blocks S2-mediated induction of proinflammatory cytokines in THP1 cells.
source: Further, inhibition of TLR2 by C29 blocked S2-mediated induction of proinflammatory cytokines in THP1 cells (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 5G using TLR2 inhibitor C29.

claim: C29 inhibits S-mediated induction of cytokines and chemokines in Calu3 cells.
source: C29 also inhibited S-mediated induction of cytokines and chemokines in Calu3 cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Concentrations of IL-6, IL-1β, and TNFα are elevated following administration of S proteins in WT mice.
source: The concentrations of IL-6, IL-1β, and TNFα were elevated following administration of S proteins in WT mice, whereas no such induction was observed in Tlr2−/− mice (Figure 5H).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo ELISA data in Figure 5H.

claim: No induction of IL-6, IL-1β, and TNFα is observed in Tlr2−/− mice following administration of S proteins.
source: The concentrations of IL-6, IL-1β, and TNFα were elevated following administration of S proteins in WT mice, whereas no such induction was observed in Tlr2−/− mice (Figure 5H).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo ELISA data in Figure 5H.

claim: TLR2 is an innate immune sensor for SARS-CoV-2 S protein.
source: These data suggest that TLR2 is an innate immune sensor for SARS-CoV-2 S protein, and recognition of S protein by TLR2 leads to the activation of NF-κB and induction of inflammatory mediators.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experiments showing TLR2-dependent responses to S protein.

claim: Recognition of S protein by TLR2 leads to the activation of NF-κB and induction of inflammatory mediators.
source: These data suggest that TLR2 is an innate immune sensor for SARS-CoV-2 S protein, and recognition of S protein by TLR2 leads to the activation of NF-κB and induction of inflammatory mediators.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experiments showing TLR2-dependent NF-κB activation and cytokine production.

claim: TLR2 forms a heterodimer with either TLR1 or TLR6 on the cell surface that promotes ligand binding and propagation of signaling.
source: It is known that TLR2 forms a heterodimer with either TLR1 or TLR6 on the cell surface that promotes ligand binding and propagation of signaling to the downstream kinases (Buwitt-Beckmann et al., 2006; Chang et al., 2007; Farhat et al., 2008; Jin et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to published literature.

claim: S1, S2, and S-tri activate NF-κB in HEK-Blue-TLR2, HEK-Blue-TLR1/2, and HEK-Blue-TLR2/6 cells.
source: When we stimulated reporter HEK-Blue cells with S1, S2, or S-tri, all three spike proteins activated NF-κB in HEK-Blue-TLR2, HEK-Blue-TLR1/2, and HEK-Blue-TLR2/6 cells, but not in HEK-Blue-Null and HEK-Blue-TLR4 cells (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: This is supported by reporter assay data in Figure 6A and B.

claim: S1, S2, and S-tri do not activate NF-κB in HEK-Blue-Null and HEK-Blue-TLR4 cells.
source: When we stimulated reporter HEK-Blue cells with S1, S2, or S-tri, all three spike proteins activated NF-κB in HEK-Blue-TLR2, HEK-Blue-TLR1/2, and HEK-Blue-TLR2/6 cells, but not in HEK-Blue-Null and HEK-Blue-TLR4 cells (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: This is supported by reporter assay data in Figure 6A and B.

claim: HEK293T cells endogenously express TLR1 and TLR6.
source: Notably, HEK293T cells endogenously express TLR1 and TLR6 (Buwitt-Beckmann et al., 2006) therefore, HEK-Blue-TLR2 cells responded to both TLR2/1 ligand Pam3CSK4 and TRL2/6 ligand FSL1 (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to published literature.

claim: NF-κB is activated in S2 stimulated HEK-Blue-TLR2, HEK-Blue-TLR1/2, and HEK-Blue-TLR2/6 cells but not in HEK-Blue-Null and HEK-Blue-TLR4 cells.
source: As shown in Figure 6C, NF-κB was activated in S2 stimulated HEK-Blue-TLR2, HEK-Blue-TLR1/2, and HEK-Blue-TLR2/6 cells but not in HEK-Blue-Null and HEK-Blue-TLR4 cells.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data in Figure 6C.

claim: S-induced expression of IL6 and IL1B is similar in HEK-Blue-TLR2, HEK-Blue-TLR2/1, and HEK-Blue-TLR2/6 cells.
source: Consistently, the S-induced expression of IL6 and IL1B was similar in HEK-Blue-TLR2, HEK-Blue-TLR2/1, and HEK-Blue-TLR2/6 cells (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data in Figure 6D.

claim: C29 completely blocks S-mediated NF-κB activation in HEK-Blue-TLR2, HEK-Blue-TLR1/2, and HEK-Blue-TLR2/6 cells.
source: C29 completely blocked S-mediated NF-κB activation in HEK-Blue-TLR2, HEK-Blue-TLR1/2, and HEK-Blue-TLR2/6 cells (Figure 6E and F), further confirming the essential role of TLR2 in S-mediated innate immune response.
evidence: This is supported by reporter assay data in Figure 6E and F.

claim: No activation of the reporter gene is observed in HEK-Blue-TLR2 or HEK-Blue-TLR4 cells stimulated with M, N, and E proteins.
source: Notably, no activation of the reporter gene was observed in HEK-Blue-TLR2 or HEK-Blue-TLR4 cells stimulated with M, N, and E proteins (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A, B), further confirming that S, but not other structural proteins, is primarily responsible for the inflammatory response.
evidence: This is supported by reporter assay data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: TLR1-KO and TLR6-KO RAW264.7 cells show no defect in S-induced inflammatory responses.
source: On stimulation of null or different TLR knockout cells with S2, TLR1-KO and TLR6-KO cells showed no defect in the S-induced inflammatory responses (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data in Figure 6G.

claim: TLR1 and TLR6 double KO RAW264.7 cells fail to induce cytokines during stimulation with S protein.
source: Interestingly, TLR1 and TLR6 double KO cells failed to induce any cytokine during stimulation with S protein (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data in Figure 6G.

claim: TLR2 requires dimerization with either TLR1 or TLR6 for sensing S protein and inducing inflammatory responses.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that TLR2 requires dimerization with either TLR1 or TLR6 for sensing S protein and inducing subsequent inflammatory responses.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experiments with TLR knockout cells and HEK-Blue reporter cells.

claim: Both SARS-CoV-2 infection and aberrant host immune responses are responsible for COVID-19 pathogenesis.
source: Both SARS-CoV-2 infection and aberrant host immune responses are responsible for COVID-19 pathogenesis (Vabret et al., 2020; Tay et al., 2020; Blanco-Melo et al., 2020; Grant et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Non-surviving COVID-19 patients exhibited a massive influx of macrophages and neutrophils, but reduced T cells in their blood.
source: Non-surviving COVID-19 patients exhibited a massive influx of macrophages and neutrophils, but reduced T cells in their blood (Liao et al., 2020), pointing to the association of hyperactivation of innate immune cells with COVID-19 pathogenesis.
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: The innate immune response is heightened in the lung of COVID-19 patients.
source: Indeed, the innate immune response is heightened in the lung of COVID-19 patients (Zhou et al., 2020a; Xiong et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The type I interferon response is attenuated in COVID-19 patients and SARS-CoV-2 infected cells.
source: Interestingly, the type I interferon response is attenuated in COVID-19 patients and SARS-CoV-2 infected cells (Blanco-Melo et al., 2020; Hadjadj et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Transcriptomic analysis of bronchoalveolar lavage fluid and PBMCs of COVID-19 patients demonstrated higher expression of proinflammatory cytokines and chemokines, but not type I interferons.
source: Transcriptomic analysis of bronchoalveolar lavage fluid and PBMCs of COVID-19 patients also demonstrated higher expression of proinflammatory cytokines and chemokines, but not type I interferons (Xiong et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Macrophages and dendritic cells infected by SARS-CoV-1 produce chemokines CXCL10 and CCL2, but not type I interferons.
source: However, previous studies on SARS-CoV-1, which share 80% similarity with SARS-CoV-2, showed that macrophages and dendritic cells infected by SARS-CoV-1 produce chemokines CXCL10 and CCL2, but not type I interferons (Cheung et al., 2005; Law et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Several structural and non-structural proteins of SARS-CoV including M, N, PLP, ORF3b, ORF6, and NSP1 inhibit type I interferon signaling.
source: Lack of an interferon response can be explained by the fact that several structural and non-structural proteins including M, N, PLP, ORF3b, ORF6, and NSP1 inhibit type I interferon signaling (Siu et al., 2014; Frieman et al., 2009; Narayanan et al., 2008; Devaraj et al., 2007; Frieman et al., 2007; Kopecky-Bromberg et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: S protein of SARS-CoV-1 and SARS-CoV-2 shares similar inflammatory function.
source: Our findings suggest that S protein of SARS-CoV-1 and SARS-CoV-2 shares similar inflammatory function (Wang et al., 2007; Dosch et al., 2009).
evidence: This is inferred from the current findings and supported by citations to published literature on SARS-CoV-1.

claim: Innate immune cells like macrophages and monocytes weakly express ACE2.
source: Inflammatory responses of COVID-19 patients are mostly contributed by innate immune cells, but they weakly express ACE2 (Ropa et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: There is no strong evidence that SARS-CoV-2 infects and propagates infection in immune cells.
source: There is no strong evidence that SARS-CoV-2 infects and propagates infection in immune cells.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: TLR2 plays a critical role in host defense against many bacterial and viral infections.
source: Being a sensor for lipopeptides and lipoproteins, TLR2 plays a critical role in host defense against many bacterial and viral infections (Oliveira-Nascimento et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Ligand recognition by TLR2 involves dimerization with TLR1 or TLR6.
source: Unlike other TLRs, ligand recognition by TLR2 involves dimerization with TLR1 or TLR6 (Buwitt-Beckmann et al., 2006; Jin et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Both TLR2/1 and TLR2/6 heterodimers are involved in the inflammatory response to core and NS3 proteins of hepatitis C virus.
source: For example, both TLR2/1 and TLR2/6 heterodimers are involved in the inflammatory response to core and NS3 proteins of hepatitis C virus (Chang et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Ligation of TLR2 leads to the activation of transcription factors NF-κB and AP-1.
source: Like other MyD88-dependent TLR pathways, ligation of TLR2 leads to the activation of transcription factors NF-κB and AP-1 (Kawasaki and Kawai, 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to published literature.

claim: SARS-CoV-1 S protein activates the NF-κB pathway in human monocyte-derived macrophages.
source: SARS-CoV-1 S protein activates the NF-κB pathway in human monocyte-derived macrophages (Wang et al., 2007; Dosch et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: COVID-19 patients exhibited increased activation of the NF-κB pathway.
source: COVID-19 patients also exhibited increased activation of the NF-κB pathway (Hadjadj et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: TLR2 could be a potential therapeutic target for COVID-19.
source: Taken together, these data reveal a mechanism for the cytokine storm during SARS-CoV-2 infection and suggest that TLR2 could be a potential therapeutic target for COVID-19.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the experimental findings showing TLR2's role in S protein-induced inflammation.

claim: TLR2 or its downstream signaling adapters could be therapeutically targeted to mitigate hyperinflammatory response in COVID-19 patients.
